In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

a given Hermitian matrix is orthogonally reducible to tridiagonal (or to Hessenberg) form if and only if its eigenvalues are pairwise distinct (or if and only if it has at most two equal eigenvalues).

the orthogonal Arnoldi reduction of a given Hermitian matrix A to Hessenberg (or tridiagonal) form with bandwidth ω is possible if and only if the Krylov matrix KA is full rank, i.e., the Krylov sequence is linearly independent.
the Hessenberg reduction to small bandwidth is possible for any matrix A, but the reduction to a tridiagonal matrix is only possible under a condition that can be verified efficiently.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we provide a new and elementary proof of the Faber-Mantuffel theorem for the special case of orthogonal Hessenberg reductions.

the Arnoldi method applied to a given matrix A yields an orthogonal Hessenberg matrix of small bandwidth if and only if the matrix BA is of small bandwidth, where B is a basis of the Krylov subspace KA, and BA is the matrix representation of BA with respect to this basis.
we provide a new, more elementary proof of a well-known fact, but in the process, we also obtain a more precise statement of the theorem.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the orthogonal Hesseberg reduction with small bandwidth can be used as a tool to analyze the Arnoldi method for solving Hermitian linear systems.
the orthogonal reduction of a given Hermitian matrix to tridiagonal or Hessenberg form can be done in such a way that the resulting tridiagonal or upper Hessenberg matrices have small bandwidth.

the Faber-Mantenuffel result can be interpreted geometrically as the statement that the orthogonal Hesseberg reduction of a Hermitian matrix is optimal for the problem of minimizing the bandwidth of a Hessenberg reduction.
